name: Tu Quoque
statement: Tu quoque dismisses a claim by accusing the claimant of hypocrisy, rather than addressing whether the claim is actually true.
meaning: Tu quoque (Latin for "you, too") responds to a criticism by pointing out that the accuser is guilty of the same thing, implying this makes the original claim false or the criticism illegitimate. It is a subtype of ad hominem: instead of engaging with whether a statement is true, it attacks the speaker’s consistency or standing to make it.
mechanism: Person A asserts claim X ("smoking is unhealthy"); Person B points out A behaves inconsistently with X (A smokes), and treats this inconsistency as refuting X. The flaw is that A’s hypocrisy has no bearing on whether X is true: a claim’s truth is independent of whether the person stating it lives up to it.

examples.text: Alice argues smoking causes health problems; Bob replies that Alice smokes, implying her claim can be dismissed. Bob’s observation about Alice’s habits does nothing to refute the factual claim.

Soviet propagandists met US criticism of human-rights abuses with "And you are lynching Negroes," a tactic traced to a 1949 speech by Konstantin Simonov, deflecting the charge rather than answering it.

The Oxford English Dictionary traces the earliest known English use of "tu quoque" to John Cooke’s 1614 play The Cittie Gallant, showing the term has been recognised in English rhetoric for over four centuries.

whyItMatters: Recognising tu quoque prevents debates from derailing into character attacks that leave the original factual question unresolved; a hypocrite can still be right, and pointing out inconsistency, while sometimes rhetorically effective, is logically irrelevant to the truth of the claim.
limits: Pointing out hypocrisy is not fallacious when the argument concerns the person’s credibility, sincerity, or standing to demand a course of action rather than the independent truth of a factual claim; it becomes fallacious only when hypocrisy is used to dismiss the truth of the underlying claim.
misreadings: Tu quoque is often conflated with whataboutism, but whataboutism deflects criticism onto an unrelated wrongdoing, whereas tu quoque narrowly targets inconsistency between the accuser’s own claim and their behaviour.
origin: The Latin phrase means "you, too." The OED records its earliest English use in John Cooke’s 1614 play The Cittie Gallant; it is classified in informal logic as a form of ad hominem exploiting perceived hypocrisy.
